question: Why do we need a background job queue at all? Why not do the work inside the HTTP request?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha answer: HTTP request milliseconds mein khatam honi chahiye, lekin bahut saara kaam slow, unreliable ya retry-worthy hota hai -- email bhejna, report generate karna, third-party API call karna. Yeh sab request ke andar karoge toh user wait karega aur dependency down hui toh user ki request fail ho jayegi.

Example: user signup karta hai, hume welcome email bhejna hai. Agar email provider 5 second slow hai, toh signup API 5 second leti hai. Provider down hai toh signup hi fail -- jabki user account toh ban chuka tha. Queue ke saath: API job enqueue karti hai (ek Redis call, kuch ms), 201 return karti hai, aur worker background mein email bhejta hai. Fail hua toh worker jittered backoff ke saath retry karta hai, user ko pata bhi nahi chalta.

Chaar benefits main interview mein bolta hoon: (1) fast responses, (2) retries bina user ko wait karaye, (3) load smoothing -- spike aaya toh queue absorb kar leti hai aur workers apni speed se drain karte hain, (4) independent scaling -- API aur workers alag alag scale hote hain. Cost yeh hai ki system ab asynchronous hai: result baad mein milta hai, aur hume delivery semantics, duplicates, aur DLQ ke baare mein sochna padta hai.
why_needed: Slow ya flaky kaam ko user ke request path se hatana, aur failures ko automatic retry karna -- bina user ko block kiye.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant mein waiter order leta hai aur turant agle table pe chala jata hai; khana kitchen (worker) background mein banata hai. Waiter khud khana banane lage toh baaki tables wait karte rahenge.
how_it_works: Producer (API) job ko Redis mein serialize karke ready zset mein daalta hai. Worker processes loop mein job claim karte hain, handler chalate hain, aur ack/fail karte hain. Fail hone pe job backoff ke baad dobara run hoti hai.
in_this_project: `POST /jobs` (`api/routes.py::enqueue`) sirf `JobQueue.enqueue` call karta hai jo `enqueue.lua` chalata hai aur 201 return karta hai. Actual kaam `python -m jobqueue.worker` processes karte hain (`worker/worker.py::Worker`). `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ka pehla section 'Why a background queue' yahi reasoning likhta hai.
disadvantages: System asynchronous ho jata hai -- result baad mein
Duplicates, DLQ, monitoring ki extra complexity
Ek aur infra component (Redis) operate karna
common_mistakes: Har chhoti cheez queue mein daal dena, jabki woh 5ms ka kaam tha
Queue ko 'fire and forget' samajhna aur failures monitor na karna
follow_up_questions: How does the client learn the result of an async job?
What delivery guarantee does your queue give?
What happens if Redis is down when the API tries to enqueue?

question: What are the main components of your job queue and what does each do?
answer_hinglish:
Paanch components hain. Pehla, **API** (FastAPI, `jobqueue/main.py` + `api/routes.py`) -- producer side: jobs enqueue, status dekhna, cancel, DLQ replay, schedules, workers list. Doosra, **Redis** -- queue ki saari mechanics: job hashes, aur har queue ke liye `ready`, `delayed`, `active`, `dead`, `completed` sorted sets. Har state transition ek Lua script hai. Teesra, **worker processes** (`python -m jobqueue.worker`) -- har process N concurrent slots chalata hai, jobs claim karta hai, handler run karta hai, lease extend karta hai, heartbeat bhejta hai, expired leases reap karta hai, aur schedules fire karta hai. Chautha, **handlers** (`handlers/builtin.py`) -- actual business logic, jaise `email.send`; registry se naam se lookup hote hain. Paanchva, **Postgres** -- business side effects aur `processed_jobs` idempotency ledger, Alembic migrations ke saath.

Plus ek `dashboard.html` jo `/queues`, `/workers`, `/dlq` dikhata hai.

Main point jo main interview mein highlight karta hoon: Redis queue mechanics ke liye hai (fast, atomic), aur Postgres correctness-critical side effects ke liye (ACID). Yeh split deliberate hai -- dono ka kaam alag hai.
why_needed: Component boundaries clear hon toh failure analysis aur scaling discussion easy ho jata hai.
real_world_analogy: Post office: counter (API) parcel leta hai, sorting room (Redis) parcels ko racks mein rakhta hai, delivery boys (workers) parcels uthate hain, aur register (Postgres) mein entry hoti hai ki kaunsa parcel deliver ho chuka.
how_it_works: API -> enqueue.lua -> Redis zsets. Workers -> claim.lua / ack.lua / fail.lua / extend_lease.lua. Handlers -> Postgres transaction. Dashboard -> API read endpoints.
in_this_project: `ARCHITECTURE.md` ka directory map aur mermaid flowchart exactly yeh dikhata hai. `docker-compose.yml` mein services: `redis`, `postgres`, `migrate`, `api`, `worker` (3 replicas, `--concurrency 16`).
advantages: Clear separation: mechanics vs business effects
Same image, roles chosen by command
disadvantages: Do datastores operate karne padte hain
Redis aur Postgres ke beech koi shared transaction nahi
common_mistakes: API process ke andar hi workers chala dena -- deploy pe in-flight jobs aur API dono ek saath restart
follow_up_questions: Why not use only Postgres?
Why is the reaper inside the worker rather than a separate service?

question: Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery. Which one does your queue provide?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh queue **at-least-once** deti hai.

At-most-once: job ko processing se pehle hi queue se hata do aur kabhi retry mat karo. Worker beech mein mara toh job hamesha ke liye lost. Simple hai, duplicates nahi, lekin data loss.

At-least-once: job tab tak queue ki ownership mein rehti hai jab tak worker explicitly ack na kare. Worker crash hua, lease expire hui, toh job dobara deliver hogi. Kabhi job lose nahi hoti, lekin same job do baar chal sakti hai -- isliye handlers idempotent hone chahiye.

Exactly-once: har job ka effect exactly ek baar. Network ke across general case mein yeh impossible hai, kyunki worker ka "kaam ho gaya" message aur actual side effect atomic nahi ho sakte -- crash beech mein kahin bhi ho sakta hai. Practically hum isse approximate karte hain: at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer. Isse "effectively-once" bolte hain.

Is project mein claim job ko delete nahi karta, `active` zset mein lease deadline ke saath rakhta hai. Ack nahi aaya toh reaper `fail.lua` se job wapas retry mein bhejta hai. Aur `email.send` handler `processed_jobs` ledger se duplicate effect rokta hai.
why_needed: Kaunsi guarantee hai, yeh decide karta hai ki handlers ko kya likhna padega aur kaunse failures acceptable hain.
real_world_analogy: Courier: at-most-once = ek baar try, nahi mila toh parcel phek diya. At-least-once = tab tak try karo jab tak signature na mile, kabhi kabhi do baar ghanti baj jaati hai. Exactly-once = har baar perfect -- asli duniya mein guarantee nahi.
how_it_works: At-least-once ka mechanism: lease (visibility timeout) + redelivery until ack. Duplicates ka source: worker ne side effect kiya lekin ack se pehle mara, ya lease expire ho gayi jab handler abhi chal raha tha.
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ki 'Delivery semantics' table teeno ko compare karti hai aur bold mein likhti hai 'At-least-once (this project)'. Mechanism: `claim.lua` job ko `active` zset mein `deadline` score ke saath daalta hai; `JobQueue.reap_expired` expired jobs ko `fail.lua` (reason `lease_expired`) se retry karta hai.
advantages: At-least-once: jobs kabhi lose nahi hoti
Idempotency ke saath effectively-once mil jata hai
disadvantages: Har handler ko idempotent banana padta hai
Duplicate execution ka window rehta hai
common_mistakes: Bolna ki 'Redis Lua se exactly-once mil gaya' -- claim exactly-once hai, execution nahi
At-most-once ko 'safe' samajhna
follow_up_questions: When exactly can a duplicate execution happen in your system?
How do you make an external email API call idempotent?
Is claiming exactly-once even though delivery is at-least-once?

question: Why is exactly-once processing impossible in general, and how does your project approximate it?
answer_hinglish:
Impossible isliye hai kyunki side effect aur acknowledgement do alag systems mein hote hain, aur unke beech koi atomic commit nahi hai. Worker ne email bheja (ya DB row likhi), phir ack bhejne se pehle crash. Queue ko kabhi pata nahi chalega ki effect ho chuka -- uske liye job unacked hai, toh woh redeliver karegi. Ulta karo -- pehle ack, phir effect -- toh crash pe effect lost (at-most-once). Order kuch bhi rakho, crash window rahega. Yeh Two Generals problem ki family hai.

Approximation: **at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer**. Effect ke saath ek dedupe record ko SAME transaction mein commit karo. `email.send` handler ek Postgres transaction mein pehle `processed_jobs(job_id)` insert karta hai `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING job_id` se. Row wapas aayi toh pehli baar hai -> `email_outbox` mein insert. Row nahi aayi toh pehle ho chuka -> skip, `{"duplicate": true}` return. Dono insert ek hi transaction mein commit hote hain, toh "effect hua lekin ledger nahi" wali state possible hi nahi.

Proof: `test_kill_minus_nine_worker_process` real worker process ko commit ke baad kill karta hai; doosra process job finish karta hai `attempts == 2`, `duplicate is True`, aur `email_outbox` mein exactly 1 row.

Limitation honestly: yeh sirf database effects ke liye kaam karta hai. Real external API ke liye job id ko provider ki idempotency key ke roop mein bhejna padega.
why_needed: Interviewers check karte hain ki aap 'exactly-once' marketing aur actual guarantee mein fark samajhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Bank cheque: cashier ek register mein cheque number likh deta hai paisa dene ke saath hi. Wahi cheque dobara aaye toh register dekh ke mana kar deta hai.
how_it_works: Ledger PK conflict = duplicate detection. Effect + ledger ek transaction mein = atomic. Redelivery harmless ban jati hai.
in_this_project: `handlers/builtin.py::send_email` -- `insert(ProcessedJob)...on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["job_id"]).returning(ProcessedJob.job_id)`, aur `EmailOutbox` insert, dono `async with ctx.sessionmaker() as session, session.begin():` ke andar. `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` ka 'duplicate-execution window' section teen cases list karta hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: jobqueue/handlers/builtin.py
async with ctx.sessionmaker() as session, session.begin():
    claimed = await session.execute(
        insert(ProcessedJob).values(job_id=ctx.job.id, job_type=ctx.job.type, attempt=ctx.attempt)
        .on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["job_id"]).returning(ProcessedJob.job_id))
    if claimed.scalar_one_or_none() is None:
        existing = await session.scalar(select(EmailOutbox.id).where(EmailOutbox.job_id == ctx.job.id))
        return {"duplicate": True, "email_id": existing}
    ...  # insert EmailOutbox in the same transaction
advantages: Duplicate deliveries harmless ho jati hain
disadvantages: Sirf usi DB ke effects ke liye atomic hai jahan ledger hai
Ledger table grow karti rehti hai -- cleanup chahiye
common_mistakes: Ledger insert aur effect alag transactions mein karna
Ledger check SELECT se karna (race) instead of INSERT ON CONFLICT
follow_up_questions: What if the side effect is an HTTP call to a payment provider?
How would you clean up the processed_jobs table?
What if two workers run the same job at the same time?

question: What is a Redis sorted set and why is it a good fit for a job queue?
answer_hinglish:
Sorted set (ZSET) ek collection hai jisme har member unique hota hai aur uske saath ek numeric score hota hai. Redis members ko score ke order mein rakhta hai (internally skiplist + hash), toh "sabse chhota score wala do" (`ZPOPMIN`), "score X se kam wale sab do" (`ZRANGEBYSCORE`), aur add/remove sab O(log n) hain.

Job queue ke liye yeh perfect hai kyunki humein teen alag ordering chahiye, aur teeno ek score se express ho jati hain:
1. `ready` zset -- score = `(9 - priority) * 1e13 + seq`. `ZPOPMIN` sabse urgent, phir sabse purani job deta hai.
2. `delayed` zset -- score = `run_at` ms. `ZRANGEBYSCORE -inf now` se due jobs mil jati hain.
3. `active` zset -- score = lease deadline ms. Reaper `ZRANGEBYSCORE -inf now` se expired leases dhoondta hai.
Plus `dead` (died-at time) aur `completed` (finished time, capped).

Plain Redis LIST (LPUSH/BRPOP) sirf FIFO deta hai -- priority, delay, ya lease deadline nahi. Isliye zsets. Member job id hai, aur actual job data alag hash `jq:job:{id}` mein. Zset mein sirf id rakhne se zset chhota rehta hai aur job data ek jagah.
why_needed: Priority, scheduling aur lease timeout -- teeno ko efficiently implement karne ke liye ordered data structure chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Hospital ki waiting list jisme har patient ke naam ke aage ek token number hai; doctor hamesha sabse chhota token bulata hai. Emergency patient ko chhota number de do toh woh aage aa jata hai.
how_it_works: Skiplist O(log n) insert/delete/rank deta hai; hash table O(1) member lookup (ZSCORE, ZREM). ZPOPMIN atomically min member nikal deta hai.
in_this_project: `core/queue.py` ka module docstring poora key layout deta hai: `jq:q:{queue}:ready`, `:delayed`, `:active`, `:dead`, `:completed`. `claim.lua` mein `ZPOPMIN KEYS[1]` aur `ZRANGEBYSCORE KEYS[2] -inf now`.
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/claim.lua
local due = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[2], '-inf', now, 'LIMIT', 0, tonumber(ARGV[4]))
...
local popped = redis.call('ZPOPMIN', KEYS[1])
advantages: Ek structure se priority, delay aur timeout teeno
Range queries due/expired items ke liye
disadvantages: List se zyada memory per item
Blocking pop (BZPOPMIN) batch claim ke saath mix karna mushkil
common_mistakes: Job ka poora payload zset member mein daal dena -- update/lookup mushkil
LIST use karke priority ke liye multiple lists aur polling ka jugaad
follow_up_questions: Why not use Redis Streams with consumer groups?
What is the complexity of ZPOPMIN?

question: What is a Redis Lua script and why does every state transition in this queue use one?
answer_hinglish:
Redis Lua script (EVAL/EVALSHA) server pe chalta hai, aur Redis single-threaded command execution ki wajah se script ke chalte waqt koi doosra command beech mein nahi aa sakta. Matlab script ke andar ke saare commands ek atomic unit ki tarah chalte hain.

Job queue mein har transition multi-step hai. Claim ko dekho: ready se pop karo, attempts badhao, status `active` karo, lease deadline set karo, active zset mein daalo. Agar yeh paanch alag commands client se bhejo aur worker teesre command ke baad crash ho jaye, toh job ready se nikal chuki hai lekin active mein kabhi nahi gayi -- job hamesha ke liye gayab. Reaper bhi nahi dhoondh payega kyunki woh sirf active zset scan karta hai.

Isliye design decision #1 (`ARCHITECTURE.md`): "One Lua script per transition -> no partial states". Is project mein aath scripts hain: `enqueue`, `claim`, `ack`, `fail`, `extend_lease`, `requeue_dead`, `cancel`, `schedule_tick`. Plus Lua ke andar check-then-act bhi safe hai -- jaise `ack.lua` pehle status aur attempts check karta hai, phir update. Client side pe yahi karte toh race condition hoti.

Ek caution: script Redis ko block karta hai, isliye scripts chhote aur bounded rakhe hain (`max_promote` 100, `max_jobs` = free slots).
why_needed: Multi-step state changes ko crash-safe aur race-free banane ke liye.
real_world_analogy: Bank locker mein do chabiyan ek saath ghumani padti hain; ya toh dono ghoomengi ya koi nahi -- beech wali state hoti hi nahi.
how_it_works: Redis script ko ek command ki tarah execute karta hai; script ke dauran event loop doosre clients ko serve nahi karta. redis-py `register_script` SHA cache karta hai aur EVALSHA bhejta hai, NOSCRIPT pe EVAL fallback.
in_this_project: `core/queue.py` mein `SCRIPTS = ["enqueue", "claim", "ack", "fail", "extend_lease", "requeue_dead", "cancel", "schedule_tick"]` aur constructor mein `redis.register_script(...)` har ek ke liye. Saare scripts `jobqueue/core/lua/` mein.
code_example:
# real: jobqueue/core/queue.py
SCRIPTS = ["enqueue", "claim", "ack", "fail", "extend_lease", "requeue_dead", "cancel", "schedule_tick"]
...
self._s = {n: redis.register_script((_LUA / f"{n}.lua").read_text(encoding="utf-8")) for n in SCRIPTS}
advantages: Ek round trip mein poora kaam
disadvantages: Long script poore Redis ko block karta hai
Lua debugging mushkil
Cluster mein saari keys same slot mein honi chahiye
common_mistakes: Script mein unbounded loop (jaise saari delayed jobs promote karna)
Socha ki MULTI/EXEC se check-then-act ho jayega -- MULTI mein reads ka result beech mein nahi milta
follow_up_questions: Why not MULTI/EXEC or WATCH?
What happens if a Lua script errors halfway?
How does Redis Cluster affect these scripts?

question: What is a dead letter queue and when does a job end up there in your system?
answer_hinglish:
Dead letter queue (DLQ) woh jagah hai jahan woh jobs jaati hain jo baar baar try karne ke baad bhi succeed nahi hui. Maksad: (1) poison message queue ko infinite loop mein na fasaye, (2) failed job ka data aur errors lose na hon, taaki engineer bug fix karke replay kar sake.

Is project mein job teen raaston se DLQ (`jq:q:{queue}:dead` zset, score = died-at ms) mein jaati hai, sab `fail.lua` se:
1. Attempts khatam: `attempts >= max_attempts` (default 5). Yeh handler error, timeout, ya lease expiry -- kisi bhi reason se ho sakta hai.
2. `PermanentError`: handler ne explicitly bola ki retry se fix nahi hoga (galat recipient), toh `force_dead = '1'` aur remaining attempts skip.
3. Unknown job type: worker ko handler nahi mila toh `PermanentError` raise hota hai -> seedha dead.

Dead job ka hash expire nahi hota (ack ki tarah EXPIRE nahi lagta), status `dead`, aur `jq:job:{id}:errors` list mein last 20 attempts ke errors rehte hain (`attempt`, `at`, `reason`, `error`). Replay: `POST /dlq/{id}/requeue` ya `/dlq/requeue-all?queue=&type=` -> `requeue_dead.lua` job ko attempts 0 karke ready mein daalta hai. Dashboard pe Requeue button bhi hai.
why_needed: Bina DLQ ke ya toh failed jobs hamesha retry hoti rahengi (resource waste) ya chupchaap gayab ho jayengi (data loss).
real_world_analogy: Post office ka 'undelivered mail' section: address galat hai toh parcel wahan rakh dete hain; customer aake address theek kare toh dobara dispatch.
how_it_works: fail.lua: agar force_dead != '1' aur attempts < max_attempts -> delayed (retry). Warna status dead, ZADD dead now id, stats.dead++.
in_this_project: `fail.lua` lines 22-34. Test `test_retry_with_backoff_then_dead_letter`: max_attempts=3, outcomes `["retry", "retry", "dead"]`, `len(job.errors) == 3`, phir `requeue_dead` ke baad claim pe token 1. API test `test_dlq_requeue_flow` 409 check karta hai jab job dead nahi.
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/fail.lua (tail)
redis.call('HSET', jk, 'status', 'dead', 'finished_at', now)
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[3], now, ARGV[2])
redis.call('HINCRBY', KEYS[4], 'dead', 1)
advantages: Poison messages ka infinite loop band
disadvantages: DLQ ko koi dekhta nahi toh silently jobs pile hoti hain
Dead hashes expire nahi hote -- memory grow
common_mistakes: DLQ pe alert na lagana
Bug fix kiye bina requeue-all chala dena -- sab wapas DLQ
follow_up_questions: How do you safely replay 10,000 dead jobs?
Difference between poison message and PermanentError?

question: What does idempotency mean, and where does this project apply it?
answer_hinglish:
Idempotent operation woh hai jise ek baar karo ya das baar, final result same rahe. Distributed systems mein retries aur redeliveries normal hain, isliye idempotency safety net hai.

Is project mein do alag jagah idempotency hai, aur interview mein yeh fark bolna important hai:

1. **Enqueue idempotency (producer side)**: client ne `POST /jobs` bheja, network timeout hua, client ko nahi pata job bani ya nahi, toh woh retry karta hai. Bina protection ke do jobs ban jayengi -> do emails. Solution: `idempotency_key`. `enqueue.lua` `jq:idem:{key}` check karta hai; key pehle se hai toh existing job id return, kuch enqueue nahi. API 201 ki jagah 200 deti hai. Key 24h TTL ke saath (`idempotency_ttl_seconds`).

2. **Processing idempotency (consumer side)**: at-least-once ki wajah se same job do baar chal sakti hai. `email.send` handler `processed_jobs` ledger mein job id insert karta hai side effect ke saath same transaction mein; dobara aaye toh conflict -> skip.

Teesra chhota example: `schedule_tick` per-slot idempotency key `schedule:{name}:{next_run_ms}` lagata hai taaki ek schedule slot do jobs na bana sake.

Dono milke end-to-end safety dete hain: duplicate request -> ek job; duplicate execution -> ek effect.
why_needed: Network retries aur at-least-once redelivery duplicates create karte hain; idempotency unhe harmless banati hai.
real_world_analogy: Lift ka button: ek baar dabao ya paanch baar, lift ek hi baar aayegi.
how_it_works: Enqueue: GET idem key -> exists? return old id : SET key EX ttl + create job. Consume: INSERT ledger ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING -> empty means already done.
in_this_project: `enqueue.lua` lines 8-12, `tests/test_queue_core.py::test_enqueue_idempotency_key` (same id, `ready == 1`), `tests/test_api.py::test_idempotent_enqueue_returns_200_and_same_job`, aur `handlers/builtin.py::send_email`.
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/enqueue.lua
if KEYS[4] ~= '' then
  local existing = redis.call('GET', KEYS[4])
  if existing then return {existing, 0} end
  redis.call('SET', KEYS[4], ARGV[2], 'EX', tonumber(ARGV[7]))
end
advantages: Client safely retry kar sakta hai
disadvantages: Idempotency key TTL ke baad same key nayi job bana degi
Client ko meaningful key choose karni padti hai
common_mistakes: Random UUID ko idempotency key banana har retry pe naya -- useless
Sirf ek side (producer ya consumer) pe idempotency lagana
follow_up_questions: What happens after the 24h idempotency TTL expires?
Should the idempotency key be scoped per tenant?

question: Walk me through the lifecycle (state machine) of a job.
answer_hinglish:
Job ke states `core/models.py::JobStatus` mein hain: `queued`, `delayed`, `active`, `succeeded`, `dead`, `cancelled`.

Flow:
- Enqueue: agar `delay_seconds` ya future `run_at_ms` hai toh `delayed` (delayed zset, score run_at), warna `queued` (ready zset).
- `delayed -> queued`: jab run_at aa jaye, `claim.lua` ke andar promotion hoti hai.
- `queued -> active`: claim. Attempts++ hota hai, lease deadline set, active zset mein.
- `active -> succeeded`: `ack.lua`, sirf agar token (attempt) match kare. Hash pe retention EXPIRE lag jata hai.
- `active -> delayed`: fail / timeout / lease expired, aur attempts abhi baaki -> backoff ke saath delayed mein.
- `active -> dead`: attempts khatam ya `PermanentError`.
- `queued/delayed -> cancelled`: `DELETE /jobs/{id}`. Active job cancel nahi hoti (409).
- `dead -> queued`: DLQ requeue, attempts reset.

Interesting cheez: retry ke liye alag state nahi hai -- retry bas `delayed` hai backoff ke saath. Scheduling aur retry dono same delayed zset reuse karte hain, aur dono ki promotion claim mein hoti hai. Har arrow exactly ek Lua script hai, isliye job kabhi "do states ke beech" nahi atakti.
why_needed: State machine samjhe bina failure handling, monitoring aur API behaviour explain nahi kar sakte.
real_world_analogy: Online order tracking: placed -> scheduled -> out for delivery -> delivered, ya returned to warehouse (retry) ya cancelled.
how_it_works: Status hash field `status` mein hai aur job id exactly ek zset mein hoti hai (ready/delayed/active/dead/completed) -- dono ek hi script mein update hote hain.
in_this_project: `ARCHITECTURE.md` ka `stateDiagram-v2` poora flow dikhata hai. Enum: `JobStatus` in `core/models.py`. `list_ids` status ko zset kind pe map karta hai (QUEUED->ready, ACTIVE->active, SUCCEEDED->completed...).
code_example:
# real: jobqueue/core/models.py
class JobStatus(StrEnum):
    QUEUED = "queued"        # in the ready zset, waiting for a worker
    DELAYED = "delayed"      # scheduled for later (run_at) or waiting for a retry backoff
    ACTIVE = "active"        # leased by a worker
    SUCCEEDED = "succeeded"
    DEAD = "dead"            # exhausted retries -> dead letter queue
    CANCELLED = "cancelled"
advantages: Retry aur schedule ek hi mechanism
disadvantages: Cancelled jobs ka koi zset nahi -- list nahi kar sakte
Active job ko cancel karne ka koi tareeka nahi
common_mistakes: Status field update karna lekin zset membership bhool jana (do sources of truth out of sync)
follow_up_questions: Why can't you cancel an active job?
Where is the 'retrying' state?

question: What is a visibility timeout / lease, and why doesn't claim simply delete the job?
answer_hinglish:
Lease ka matlab: worker ko job ek limited time ke liye "udhaar" milti hai. Claim pe job delete nahi hoti -- `active` zset mein jaati hai jiska score lease deadline (ms) hai. Worker time pe ack kare toh job succeeded. Worker mar gaya ya atak gaya toh deadline nikal jati hai, aur reaper job ko wapas retry mein daal deta hai. SQS isko visibility timeout bolta hai.

Delete kyun nahi? Agar claim pe hi delete kar diya aur worker crash hua toh job ka koi record nahi -- woh at-most-once ho gaya, job lost. Lease ke saath queue ownership tab tak rakhti hai jab tak explicit ack na aaye.

Is project mein lease ka formula `claim.lua` mein: `lease_ms = min(timeout_ms, max_lease_ms) + lease_grace_ms`. Default `max_lease_ms` 30000 aur grace 5000, toh 1 ghante ki job ko bhi ~35s ka lease milta hai. Worker zinda hai toh `_keep_lease` har `lease/3` time pe `extend_lease.lua` call karke deadline aage badhata hai. Faayda: crash detection ~35s mein, job timeout chahe 1 ghanta ho.

Test `test_visibility_timeout_reaper_and_fencing`: timeout 10s, grace 1000 -> `lease == 11_000`; `lease - 1` pe reaper kuch nahi karta, `lease + 1` pe `retry == 1`.
why_needed: Worker crash hone pe jobs ko recover karne ka yahi mechanism hai -- at-least-once ki neev.
real_world_analogy: Library book: aap 14 din ke liye issue karte ho, renew karte raho toh rakh sakte ho; renew nahi kiya aur gayab ho gaye toh library book ko 'lost' maan ke doosre ko de deti hai.
how_it_works: active zset score = deadline. Reaper: ZRANGEBYSCORE active -inf now -> fail.lua(reason=lease_expired). Extension: ZADD active new_deadline id.
in_this_project: `claim.lua` lines 31-36 lease compute aur `ZADD KEYS[3] deadline id`. `Worker._keep_lease` extension cadence. Config: `config.py` `max_lease_ms: int = 30000`, `lease_grace_ms: int = 5000`.
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/claim.lua
local timeout_ms = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', jk, 'timeout_ms') or '30000')
local lease_ms = math.min(timeout_ms, tonumber(ARGV[5])) + tonumber(redis.call('HGET', jk, 'lease_grace_ms') or '5000')
local attempt = redis.call('HINCRBY', jk, 'attempts', 1)
local deadline = now + lease_ms
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[3], deadline, id)
advantages: Crashed worker ki jobs automatically recover
Detection time job timeout se independent
disadvantages: Lease extension traffic
Blocked event loop extension miss kare toh duplicate execution
common_mistakes: Lease = job timeout rakhna (1h job ka crash 1h baad pata chalega)
Lease bina extension ke bahut chhota rakhna -- healthy jobs bhi redeliver
follow_up_questions: Why is the lease capped at 30s?
What if the worker is alive but its lease still expires?
Who runs the reaper?

question: What is a zombie worker and how do fencing tokens protect against it?
answer_hinglish:
Zombie worker woh hai jo mara nahi, sirf ruka tha -- GC pause, laptop sleep, network partition, ya blocked event loop. Uski lease expire ho gayi, reaper ne job retry mein daali, aur worker B ne job claim kar li (attempt 2). Ab worker A jaagta hai aur bolta hai "done, ack!". Agar hum maan lein toh B ka result overwrite ho sakta hai, ya A ka purana `fail` job ko galat state mein daal dega.

Lease akela kaafi nahi hai kyunki A ko pata hi nahi ki uski lease chali gayi. Solution: **fencing token** -- ek monotonically badhne wala number jo har lease ke saath milta hai, aur har write pe check hota hai. Is project mein token = `attempts` counter. `claim.lua` `HINCRBY attempts 1` karta hai aur wahi value worker ko deta hai. `ack.lua`, `fail.lua`, `extend_lease.lua` teeno pehle check karte hain: `status == 'active'` aur `attempts == token`. A ka token 1, current 2 -> ack 0 return, fail `'stale'`, extend 0.

Worker side pe stale ack aaye toh `stats.stale_acks += 1` aur `stale_ack_rejected` warning log. Test `test_visibility_timeout_reaper_and_fencing` exactly yeh teen rejections assert karta hai, phir B ka ack True.

Honest limitation: fencing sirf Redis state ko protect karta hai. A ne jo side effect Postgres mein kiya, woh fencing se nahi rukta -- woh idempotency ledger rokta hai.
why_needed: Lease expiry ke baad purane owner ki late writes ko reject karna, warna state corrupt hoti hai.
real_world_analogy: Hotel room key card: check-out ke baad naya guest aaya toh room ka lock naye code pe set ho jata hai; purana card ab kaam nahi karta, chahe purana guest wapas aa jaye.
how_it_works: Token issued at claim (attempts++). Every mutating script compares stored attempts with presented token inside Lua, so check and write are atomic.
in_this_project: `ack.lua` line 8: `if state[1] ~= 'active' or state[2] ~= ARGV[3] then return 0 end`. `Worker._execute` mein `else` branch stale ack ko count karta hai. `ARCHITECTURE.md` decision #2: 'Attempt number as fencing token -> monotonic, already stored, no extra key.'
code_example:
# real: tests/test_queue_core.py (trimmed)
job_b, token_b = await q.claim("default", "B", now_ms=T0 + lease + 10_000)
assert token_b == 2 and job_b.id == jid
assert await q.ack(job_a, token_a, "late", now_ms=T0 + lease + 10_001) is False    # zombie rejected
assert await q.fail(job_a, token_a, "late", now_ms=T0 + lease + 10_001) == "stale"
assert await q.extend_lease(job_a, token_a, 5000, now_ms=T0 + lease + 10_001) is False
advantages: Zombie writes Redis state corrupt nahi kar sakti
Koi extra key nahi -- attempts already stored
disadvantages: External side effects ko fence nahi karta
DLQ requeue attempts reset karta hai -- token ki monotonicity ka edge case
common_mistakes: Sirf worker_id compare karna -- same worker ka purana attempt bhi zombie ho sakta hai
Check Python mein karna aur write Lua mein -- race
follow_up_questions: Why is the attempt counter safe as a token even though DLQ requeue resets it?
How would you fence writes to Postgres too?

question: Explain the idempotent consumer pattern as implemented in the email.send handler.
answer_hinglish:
Idempotent consumer ka idea: consumer har message ki identity ko ek durable ledger mein record kare, aur yeh record side effect ke saath atomically commit ho. Duplicate aaye toh ledger bata deta hai "ho chuka", skip.

`email.send` step by step:
1. Payload validation: `to` missing ya `@` nahi -> `PermanentError` (retry bekaar).
2. `async with ctx.sessionmaker() as session, session.begin():` -- ek Postgres transaction.
3. `INSERT INTO processed_jobs(job_id, job_type, attempt) ... ON CONFLICT (job_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING job_id`.
4. Row wapas nahi aayi -> kisi pichle attempt ne commit kar diya tha. Existing `email_outbox.id` dhoondo aur `{"duplicate": True, "email_id": ...}` return karo -- side effect nahi.
5. Row aayi -> `email_outbox` mein insert, transaction commit.

Kyun INSERT ON CONFLICT aur SELECT-then-INSERT nahi? Kyunki do workers ek saath (zombie case) chal rahe hon toh dono SELECT mein "nahi hai" dekh lenge. INSERT pe PK constraint database level pe race resolve karta hai -- doosra insert pehle wale transaction ke commit/rollback tak wait karega aur phir conflict dekhega.

Test hook: `crash_after_commit` payload + attempt 1 pe handler commit ke baad `asyncio.sleep(3600)` -- matlab "worker commit ke baad, ack se pehle mara". Do tests isko use karte hain: in-process cancel aur real subprocess kill.
why_needed: At-least-once delivery mein duplicate execution guaranteed possible hai; yeh pattern usse harmless banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Shaadi ka gift register: gate pe naam likho aur gift do ek saath. Koi dobara aaye toh register mein naam dekh ke bolte ho 'aap toh de chuke'.
how_it_works: Primary key uniqueness + transaction atomicity. Ledger row aur effect row dono ya toh commit hote hain ya dono rollback.
in_this_project: `handlers/builtin.py::send_email` aur `db/models.py::ProcessedJob` (PK `job_id`). Tests: `test_worker.py::test_redelivery_after_crash_is_idempotent` aur `test_crash_process.py::test_kill_minus_nine_worker_process` -- dono `EmailOutbox` count == 1 assert karte hain.
advantages: Duplicate run original result report karta hai
disadvantages: Har handler ko pattern follow karna padta hai
Ledger cleanup policy chahiye
common_mistakes: Ledger ko Redis mein rakhna aur effect Postgres mein -- atomic nahi
Ledger mein job_id ki jagah random value
Duplicate pe error raise karna -- job phir retry hogi
follow_up_questions: Why return success on duplicate instead of raising?
What key would you use if the same logical email can be enqueued as two different jobs?

question: What is exponential backoff with full jitter and why do you need the jitter?
answer_hinglish:
Exponential backoff: har failure ke baad retry delay double karo -- base, 2x base, 4x base... ek max tak. Taaki failing dependency ko recover hone ka time mile. Full jitter: delay exactly yeh value nahi, balki `random(0, cap)` jahan `cap = min(max, base * 2^(attempt-1))`.

Jitter kyun? Socho database 10 second ke liye down hua aur us dauraan 1000 jobs fail hui. Bina jitter sab ka attempt 1 ka delay exactly 2s -- 1000 jobs ek hi millisecond pe retry karti hain, DB jo abhi wapas aaya tha phir gir jata hai. Phir sab 4s pe, phir 8s pe -- synchronized waves. Isko thundering herd bolte hain. Full jitter in 1000 retries ko poori window mein spread kar deta hai, toh load smooth aata hai. Yeh AWS Architecture Blog (2015) ka well-known result hai, jo `backoff.py` ke docstring mein cite hai.

Is project mein `retry_delay_ms(attempt, base_ms, max_ms, rng)` -- defaults base 2s, max 600s (`EnqueueRequest`). Per-job configurable hai. `JobQueue.fail` delay compute karke `fail.lua` ko deta hai, jo `run_at = now + delay` pe delayed zset mein daalta hai.

Test `test_backoff_is_bounded_and_jittered`: attempt 5, base 1000, max 10000 -> 16000 capped to 10000; 500 samples sab `0..10000` mein aur 400 se zyada unique values.
why_needed: Retries ko failing dependency pe synchronized hammer banne se rokna.
real_world_analogy: Concert khatam hone pe sab ek hi gate se nikle toh bhagdad; announcement karo 'apne random time pe niklo' toh crowd smooth.
how_it_works: cap = min(max_ms, base_ms * 2**(attempt-1)); delay = uniform(0, cap). Expected delay cap/2, lekin variance high.
in_this_project: `core/backoff.py::retry_delay_ms` (sirf 2 lines). `JobQueue.fail` mein `if delay_ms is None: delay_ms = retry_delay_ms(attempt, job.backoff_base_ms, job.backoff_max_ms)`.
advantages: Dependency ko recover hone ka time
disadvantages: Individual retry ka time unpredictable
Kabhi kabhi delay ~0 aa sakta hai
common_mistakes: Jitter ke bina sirf exponential
Max cap na rakhna -- attempt 20 pe delay din bhar ka
Jitter sirf +-10% -- herd phir bhi clustered
follow_up_questions: Full jitter vs equal jitter vs decorrelated jitter?
Should backoff respect a Retry-After header from the dependency?

question: What is a poison message and how does your queue stop it from looping forever?
answer_hinglish:
Poison message woh job hai jo kitni bhi baar try karo, hamesha fail hogi -- jaise payload hi corrupt hai ya code mein bug hai jo us input pe crash karta hai. Khatra: agar queue unlimited retry kare toh yeh job hamesha workers ka time khayegi, logs bharegi, aur agar retry turant ho toh doosri jobs ko starve kar degi.

Is project mein teen guard hain:
1. **`max_attempts`** (default 5, 1-50 allowed). Har claim attempts badhata hai; `fail.lua` mein `attempts < max_attempts` false hua toh job dead letter queue mein.
2. **Backoff**: har retry ke beech jittered exponential delay, toh poison job tight loop nahi banati.
3. **`PermanentError`**: agar handler pehchaan le ki input hi galat hai, woh seedha DLQ bhejta hai, baaki attempts waste nahi.

Demo: `demo.poison` handler hamesha `ValueError("cannot process this payload")` raise karta hai. Test `test_end_to_end_success_retry_poison_timeout` mein max_attempts=3 ke saath woh `DEAD` state pe pahunchti hai, `attempts == 3`, aur `last_error` mein "cannot process". Docker run mein bhi `TESTING.md` likhta hai: poison job 3 attempts ke baad dead.
why_needed: Ek kharab job poore worker pool ki capacity na kha jaye.
real_world_analogy: Vending machine mein nakli sikka: machine teen baar try karke sikka reject tray mein daal deti hai, hamesha andar-bahar nahi karti.
how_it_works: attempts counter claim pe badhta hai; fail.lua compare karta hai; limit hit -> dead zset.
in_this_project: `handlers/builtin.py::poison`, `fail.lua` line 22 condition, `EnqueueRequest.max_attempts` (`ge=1, le=50`).
code_example:
# real: jobqueue/handlers/builtin.py
@registry.task("demo.poison")
async def poison(ctx: JobContext):
    """Always fails: a poison message. Must end in the DLQ, not loop forever."""
    raise ValueError("cannot process this payload")
disadvantages: Transient lambi outage mein genuine jobs bhi DLQ mein ja sakti hain
common_mistakes: Retry ko unlimited rakhna
Error type dekhe bina sab retry karna
follow_up_questions: How would you detect that a new deploy is producing poison messages?
How is PermanentError different?

question: How does PermanentError differ from a normal exception, and why does that distinction matter?
answer_hinglish:
Normal exception ka matlab hai "shayad transient hai" -- network blip, DB timeout, rate limit. Retry se fix ho sakta hai, isliye backoff ke saath retry. `PermanentError` handler ka explicit signal hai: "retry se kuch nahi badlega" -- galat email address, unknown customer, invalid payload. Aisi job ko 5 baar retry karna (aur default backoff ke saath minutes tak) resources ki barbaadi hai aur DLQ tak pahunchne mein bhi deri.

Flow: `Worker._execute` mein `except PermanentError as exc:` branch `_fail(..., "permanent", permanent=True)` call karta hai. `JobQueue.fail` `force_dead = "1"` bhejta hai. `fail.lua` line 22: `if ARGV[8] ~= '1' and attempts < max_attempts` -- force_dead pe yeh false, seedha dead.

Do jagah use hota hai: (1) `send_email` invalid recipient pe, (2) worker khud jab job type ka handler registry mein nahi milta -- `PermanentError(f"no handler registered for job type {job.type!r}")`. Test: `test_permanent_error_skips_remaining_attempts` -- max_attempts 10 ke saath bhi pehle fail pe `"dead"`. End-to-end test mein unknown type `nope.missing` max_attempts 5 ke saath `attempts == 1` aur `last_failure_reason == "permanent"`.

Note: except order matter karta hai -- `PermanentError` generic `Exception` se pehle catch hota hai.
why_needed: Retryable aur non-retryable errors ko alag treat karna -- warna ya toh resources waste ya genuine failures retry nahi hoti.
real_world_analogy: Doctor: bukhar hai toh 'do din dawai lo, phir aana' (retry). Haddi tooti hai toh 'dawai se nahi hoga, seedha surgery' (DLQ).
how_it_works: Exception class handler ka contract hai. Worker usse map karta hai reason='permanent' + force_dead flag pe.
in_this_project: `handlers/__init__.py::PermanentError`, `worker/worker.py::_execute`, `fail.lua` ARGV[8].
disadvantages: Handler author pe depend karta hai ki sahi classify kare
common_mistakes: Har exception ko PermanentError bana dena -- transient outages bhi DLQ mein
Unknown job type ko retry karna (deploy order issue mein shayad useful, lekin yahan permanent maana)
follow_up_questions: Unknown job type during a rolling deploy -- should it really be permanent?
How would you classify HTTP 429 vs 400 from a provider?

question: How do you get priority ordering and FIFO within a priority using a single sorted set score?
answer_hinglish:
Score formula: `(9 - priority) * 1e13 + seq`. `seq` ek global counter hai (`jq:seq`, `INCR`).

Priority 0-9 hai, 9 sabse urgent. `9 - priority` se priority 9 ka band 0 ho jata hai, priority 0 ka band 9. Har band 1e13 wide hai. `ZPOPMIN` sabse chhota score deta hai -> pehle sabse urgent band. Same band ke andar `seq` decide karta hai -- jo pehle enqueue hua uska seq chhota -> FIFO.

Correctness ki do conditions: (1) seq kabhi 1e13 cross na kare, warna ek band doosre mein ghus jayega -- 10 trillion jobs, practically safe. (2) Redis zset score double (float64) hai, jo 2^53 (~9e15) tak integers exactly represent karta hai. Max score ~ 9 * 1e13 + 1e13 = 1e14, safely neeche. `DATABASE_DESIGN.md` yahi reasoning likhta hai.

Test `test_priority_then_fifo`: enqueue order low1(1), high1(9), mid(5), high2(9), low2(1); claim order `["high1", "high2", "mid", "low1", "low2"]`. `test_claim_many_returns_best_jobs_in_one_call` bhi verify karta hai ki batch mein priority-2 jobs `[2, 5, 8]` order mein aati hain.

Yahi formula teen scripts mein repeat hai: `enqueue.lua`, `claim.lua` (delayed promotion), `requeue_dead.lua`. Note: promote hone pe nayi seq milti hai, toh delayed/retried job apne priority band ke end mein jaati hai.
why_needed: Ek hi ZPOPMIN se 'sabse urgent, phir sabse purani' job O(log n) mein mil jaye -- multiple lists scan kiye bina.
real_world_analogy: Railway ticket counter: senior citizens ki line pehle, phir general -- aur har line ke andar token number order.
how_it_works: Composite key encoded in one number: high-order part = priority band, low-order part = arrival sequence.
in_this_project: `enqueue.lua` line 27: `redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], (9 - tonumber(ARGV[4])) * 1e13 + seq, ARGV[2])`. `claim.lua` line 18, `requeue_dead.lua` line 9.
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/enqueue.lua
local seq = redis.call('INCR', ARGV[1] .. 'seq')
redis.call('HSET', jobkey, 'status', 'queued', 'run_at', now)
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], (9 - tonumber(ARGV[4])) * 1e13 + seq, ARGV[2])
disadvantages: Global seq key ek hot key hai
Retry hone pe job apni original position kho deti hai
common_mistakes: Score = priority only -> same priority mein order undefined (lexicographic by member)
Score mein timestamp use karna -- same ms ke jobs ka order unstable aur clock skew
follow_up_questions: Why use a sequence instead of a timestamp?
What happens to FIFO when a job is retried?
Why does 1e13 not overflow?

question: How are delayed and scheduled (run_at) jobs implemented, and who promotes them?
answer_hinglish:
Do inputs: `delay_seconds` (relative) ya `run_at_ms` (absolute unix ms). Pydantic validator dono ek saath allow nahi karta. `JobQueue.enqueue` delay ko absolute mein convert karta hai `base + delay*1000` -- base Redis `TIME` se (`_redis_now`), ya test mein injected `now_ms`.

`enqueue.lua`: agar `run_at > now` toh status `delayed`, aur `delayed` zset mein score `run_at`. Warna seedha ready.

Promotion kaun karta hai? Koi alag scheduler process nahi. `claim.lua` ka pehla step: `ZRANGEBYSCORE delayed -inf now LIMIT 0 max_promote` (default 100), har due job ko delayed se hatao, status `queued`, nayi seq, aur ready mein priority score ke saath daalo. Phir same script mein pop. Faayda: promotion aur claim ek atomic step; alag process ka failure mode nahi; jitne workers utne promoters.

Retry backoff bhi isi delayed zset ko reuse karta hai -- `fail.lua` `run_at = now + delay` set karta hai. Toh "scheduled job" aur "retry waiting for backoff" internally same cheez hai.

Test `test_delayed_and_scheduled_jobs`: delay 10s wali job aur run_at T0+5000 wali; T0+4999 pe claim None, T0+5000 pe b, T0+10000 pe a.

Caveat: promotion sirf tab hoti hai jab koi worker us queue ko claim kar raha ho. Koi worker queue nahi sun raha toh jobs delayed hi rahengi.
why_needed: Delayed emails, reminders, aur retry backoff -- sab ko time-based release chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Post-dated cheque: bank ke tray mein date ke hisaab se rakhe hain; cashier har baar counter kholte waqt pehle due cheques nikal leta hai.
how_it_works: delayed zset score = due time; claim.lua bounded promotion -> ready; same atomic script.
in_this_project: `enqueue.lua` lines 19-28, `claim.lua` lines 10-19, `EnqueueRequest._one_schedule` validator.
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/claim.lua
local due = redis.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[2], '-inf', now, 'LIMIT', 0, tonumber(ARGV[4]))
for _, id in ipairs(due) do
  redis.call('ZREM', KEYS[2], id)
  local jk = prefix .. 'job:' .. id
  local pri = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', jk, 'priority') or '5')
  local seq = redis.call('INCR', prefix .. 'seq')
  redis.call('HSET', jk, 'status', 'queued')
  redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], (9 - pri) * 1e13 + seq, id)
end
disadvantages: Idle queue pe (no worker) promotion nahi
Precision polling interval pe depend (max ~1s idle)
Promotion max 100 per call
common_mistakes: Run_at client ke local clock se compute karna
Promotion ka loop unbounded rakhna
follow_up_questions: What if 1 million jobs become due at the same instant?
Why compute delay using Redis TIME?

question: How does the enqueue idempotency key work, and why does the API return 200 instead of 201 on a repeat?
answer_hinglish:
Problem: producer `POST /jobs` bhejta hai, Redis mein job ban gayi, lekin response network pe lost. Producer retry karta hai -> duplicate job. Solution: producer ek stable `idempotency_key` bheje, jaise `welcome-email:user-42`.

`JobQueue.enqueue` key ko `jq:idem:{key}` banata hai aur `enqueue.lua` ko KEYS[4] mein deta hai (key na ho toh empty string). Script mein: `GET` -- agar value mili toh `{existing_job_id, 0}` return, kuch enqueue nahi. Nahi mili toh `SET key job_id EX idem_ttl` (default 86400s) aur normal enqueue. Check aur set ek script mein hain, toh do parallel retries mein se exactly ek jeetega -- race nahi.

API layer: `created == False` pe `response.status_code = 200`. Semantics: 201 = "naya resource bana", 200 = "yeh raha tumhara pehle wala job". Client dono case mein same job id paata hai, toh uske liye retry fully transparent hai.

Tests: `test_enqueue_idempotency_key` (`a == b`, `created_a` True, `created_b` False, ready count 1) aur `test_idempotent_enqueue_returns_200_and_same_job` (201 then 200, same id).

Limitations jo bolni chahiye: (1) TTL ke baad same key nayi job bana degi, (2) key global hai, tenant-scoped nahi, (3) dusri request ka payload alag ho toh bhi pehli job return hoti hai -- Stripe-style "payload mismatch -> 422" check nahi hai.
why_needed: Client-side retries (timeouts) se duplicate jobs na banen.
real_world_analogy: Courier booking pe reference number: same reference se dobara book karo toh nayi booking nahi, purani ki receipt mil jati hai.
how_it_works: Atomic GET-or-SET inside Lua; job id stored as value; TTL bounds memory.
in_this_project: `core/queue.py::enqueue` `idem_key = f"{self.p}idem:{req.idempotency_key}"`, `api/routes.py::enqueue` 200 logic, config `idempotency_ttl_seconds`.
code_example:
# real: jobqueue/core/queue.py
idem_key = f"{self.p}idem:{req.idempotency_key}" if req.idempotency_key else ""
await self.r.sadd(f"{self.p}queues", req.queue)
jid, created = await self._s["enqueue"](
    keys=[self.k(req.queue, "ready"), self.k(req.queue, "delayed"), self.k(req.queue, "stats"), idem_key],
    args=[self.p, job_id, json.dumps(flat), req.priority, run_at, _now_arg(now_ms), self.idem_ttl])
disadvantages: 24h ke baad protection khatam
Payload mismatch detect nahi hota
Tenant scoping nahi
common_mistakes: Idempotency key server pe generate karna (client retry pe naya)
Check aur create alag commands mein
follow_up_questions: Should a different payload with the same key be rejected?
Why is 200 better than 409 here?

question: How are job timeouts enforced, and how is a timeout different from a lease expiry?
answer_hinglish:
Timeout worker ke andar local enforce hota hai: `result = await asyncio.wait_for(handler(ctx), timeout=job.timeout_ms / 1000)`. Time khatam -> handler coroutine cancel hota hai aur `asyncio.TimeoutError` -> `_fail(..., "timeout")` -> normal retry/DLQ path. `timeout_seconds` per job hai, default 30, max 3600.

Lease expiry alag cheez hai. Lease Redis mein hai aur tab expire hoti hai jab worker extend karna band kar de -- worker crash, process kill, network partition, ya event loop blocked. Lease expire hone pe *doosra* worker ka reaper `fail.lua` reason `lease_expired` ke saath chalata hai.

Toh difference: timeout = "worker zinda hai aur handler bahut slow hai" (worker khud report karta hai). Lease expiry = "worker se sampark toot gaya" (koi aur detect karta hai). Errors list mein `reason` field se fark dikhta hai: `timeout` vs `lease_expired`.

Ek important subtlety: `asyncio.wait_for` sirf await points pe cancel kar sakta hai. Agar handler CPU-bound hai ya `time.sleep` karta hai (`demo.cpu_block`), toh timeout fire hi nahi hoga jab tak handler loop wapas na de -- tab tak lease extensions bhi ruki hongi aur lease expiry hi bachata hai.

Test: `demo.sleep` 5s ke saath `timeout_seconds=0.2`, `max_attempts=2` -> DEAD, `last_failure_reason == "timeout"`, `attempts == 2`.
why_needed: Hung handlers slots ko hamesha ke liye na pakde rahein.
real_world_analogy: Exam hall: invigilator time pe paper le leta hai (timeout). Agar student hi gayab ho gaya toh attendance se pata chalta hai (lease).
how_it_works: wait_for creates a timer; on expiry cancels the inner task and raises TimeoutError in the awaiting coroutine.
in_this_project: `Worker._execute` mein `except asyncio.TimeoutError:` branch. Lease formula `min(timeout_ms, max_lease_ms) + grace` timeout ko bhi consider karta hai.
code_example:
# real: jobqueue/worker/worker.py (trimmed)
result = await asyncio.wait_for(handler(ctx), timeout=job.timeout_ms / 1000)
...
except asyncio.TimeoutError:
    await self._fail(job, token, f"timed out after {job.timeout_ms}ms", "timeout")
disadvantages: Blocking code pe kaam nahi karta
Cancel ke baad handler ka partial side effect reh sakta hai
common_mistakes: Timeout ko lease se confuse karna
Handler mein CancelledError swallow karna -- timeout break
follow_up_questions: What happens to a DB transaction when wait_for cancels the handler?
How would you enforce timeouts for CPU-bound work?

question: How do recurring schedules work, and how do you guarantee a schedule fires once even with many workers?
answer_hinglish:
Schedules interval-based hain (cron nahi). `POST /schedules` -> `put_schedule` `jq:schedules` hash mein `name -> {interval_ms, next_run_ms, job}` store karta hai.

Har worker `_schedule_loop` mein har 1s `tick_schedules()` chalata hai. 3 workers = 3 schedulers. Double fire kaise rukta hai? Do layers:

1. **Compare-and-advance in Lua** (`schedule_tick.lua`): schedule padho; `next_run_ms > now` toh nil. Warna `next_run` ko interval se aage badhao jab tak future mein na aa jaye, wapas likho, aur *purana* raw JSON return karo. Script atomic hai, toh pehla caller advance kar deta hai, baaki sab ko `next_run > now` dikhta hai -> nil. Yeh CAS jaisa hai lekin ek script mein.
2. **Per-slot idempotency key**: Python side `req.idempotency_key = f"schedule:{name}:{next_run_ms}"` (purane raw ka next_run_ms, matlab slot time). Agar kisi tarah do callers same slot fire karein (jaise koi future bug ya manual tick), enqueue.lua same job return karega.

No-burst: loop `while next_run <= now do next_run = next_run + interval end` -- 10 interval downtime ke baad bhi ek hi run fire hota hai, aur next_run future slot pe align.

Test `test_schedule_fires_once_even_with_many_schedulers`: 5 parallel ticks -> total 1 job; 30s baad 0; 600s jump -> 1 fire aur `next_run_ms > T0 + 600_000`.
why_needed: Har worker pe scheduler chalana HA deta hai, lekin bina coordination ke har worker job fire karega.
real_world_analogy: Office mein chai ka order: jo pehle register mein 'next order time' aage likh de, wahi order karta hai; baaki register dekh ke ruk jaate hain.
how_it_works: Atomic read-check-write in Lua = distributed compare-and-set without locks; idempotency key as second line of defence.
in_this_project: `schedule_tick.lua`, `JobQueue.tick_schedules`, `Worker._schedule_loop` (`schedule_interval=1.0`).
code_example:
-- real: jobqueue/core/lua/schedule_tick.lua
if tonumber(s.next_run_ms) > now then return nil end
local interval = tonumber(s.interval_ms)
local next_run = tonumber(s.next_run_ms)
while next_run <= now do next_run = next_run + interval end
s.next_run_ms = next_run
s.last_fired_ms = now
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], cjson.encode(s))
return raw
disadvantages: Interval-only, cron expressions nahi
Missed slots skip -- har slot chahiye toh design alag
Tick resolution ~1s
common_mistakes: Leader election ke bina har worker se seedha enqueue
Downtime ke baad saare missed runs fire karna
follow_up_questions: What if the tick advanced next_run but the worker crashed before enqueuing?
How would you support cron expressions?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Leaderless CAS vs leader election: CAS simple hai aur har worker scheduler hai; leader election (Redis lock) ek hi scheduler deta hai lekin lock expiry aur failover ka complexity aata hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Advance aur enqueue do alag steps hain: script ne next_run aage kiya, phir Python enqueue karne se pehle crash -> woh slot miss. Yeh documented nahi hai lekin code se clear hai; fix: enqueue ko bhi same Lua script mein le aao.
advanced.alternatives: Leader election + in-memory cron (APScheduler), Kubernetes CronJob, ya Postgres row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a schedules table.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Schedules ki sankhya badhi (10k) toh har worker har second saari HKEYS scan karega -- N workers x 10k EVALSHA. Better: schedules ko next_run_ms score wale zset mein rakho aur sirf due wale ZRANGEBYSCORE se uthao.
advanced.production_improvements: Enqueue ko schedule_tick.lua ke andar move karo (atomic fire), cron syntax, last_fired metrics, aur 'catch-up' mode per schedule.

question: Heartbeats vs leases: which one actually recovers a crashed worker's jobs in your design, and why?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha answer: jobs **leases** se recover hoti hain, heartbeats se nahi. Heartbeat sirf observability ke liye hai.

Heartbeat: har worker `_heartbeat_loop` mein har 5s (default `heartbeat_interval`) `jq:workers` hash mein apni info (running jobs, processed, failed, stale_acks, last_heartbeat) likhta hai, aur `jq:worker:{id}:alive` key `px = interval * 3000` ms TTL ke saath set karta hai. `GET /workers` us key ke exist karne se `alive` decide karta hai. Dashboard 'STALE Ns' dikhata hai.

Lease recovery heartbeats pe kyun nahi? Kyunki worker-level liveness job-level correctness ke liye galat granularity hai. Worker zinda ho sakta hai lekin ek specific job atak gayi ho (blocked loop sirf us waqt). Ya heartbeat key network glitch se expire ho jaye jab jobs theek chal rahi hon. Agar "worker dead -> uski saari jobs requeue" karte toh yeh decision non-atomic hota aur races aate. Lease per-job hai, deadline Redis mein hai, aur reaper `fail.lua` mein atomically deadline recheck karta hai -- zyada precise aur race-free.

`FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` row 13 yahi bolta hai: "its jobs are recovered by leases, not by heartbeats". Test `test_workers_endpoint_reports_stale` ek ghost worker inject karta hai jiska last_heartbeat 60s purana hai aur key nahi hai -> `alive is False`.
why_needed: Failure detection aur recovery ko alag samajhna -- monitoring signal aur correctness mechanism alag hote hain.
real_world_analogy: Factory: security guard attendance register (heartbeat) dekh ke batata hai kaun aaya. Lekin machine pe kaam kisne chhoda, yeh har machine ka apna timer (lease) batata hai.
how_it_works: Heartbeat: periodic SET with TTL (3x interval) + info hash. Lease: per-job deadline in active zset, renewed by _keep_lease, enforced by reaper.
in_this_project: `Worker._heartbeat_loop`, `api/routes.py::workers`, `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` row 13.
code_example:
# real: jobqueue/worker/worker.py
pipe = self.q.r.pipeline(transaction=False)
pipe.hset(f"{self.q.p}workers", self.id, json.dumps(info))
pipe.set(f"{self.q.p}worker:{self.id}:alive", 1, px=max(int(self.heartbeat_interval * 3000), 1))
await pipe.execute()
advantages: Heartbeats debugging aur alerting ke liye
No race between 'worker dead' decision and job ownership
disadvantages: Do mechanisms maintain karne padte hain
Crashed worker ki entry `jq:workers` mein reh jati hai -- manual `DELETE /workers/{id}`
common_mistakes: Heartbeat miss pe worker ki saari jobs blindly requeue karna
Heartbeat TTL = interval (ek late beat pe false alarm)
follow_up_questions: Why is the TTL 3x the interval?
How would you auto-clean dead worker entries?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Lease per-job, precise, atomic; heartbeat per-worker, cheap, monitoring-friendly. Dono ka combination standard hai (Sidekiq, Celery bhi aisa hi karte hain).
advanced.failure_scenarios: Heartbeat loop crash (jaise TTL bug) -> dashboard pe worker dead dikhega jabki jobs chal rahi hain. Lease-based recovery isse affected nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Worker registry with session (ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes / etcd leases) jahan session expiry pe ownership automatically release hoti hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 1000 workers x heartbeat har 5s = 200 writes/s -- Redis ke liye trivial. Workers hash bada hoga; GET /workers har worker pe EXISTS karta hai (N round trips) -- pipeline karna padega.
advanced.production_improvements: Dead worker entries ko auto-prune karo (alive key missing + last_heartbeat > X), aur heartbeat staleness pe alert lagao.
